78225.subject: Avalanche L1 Explained: Why Build a Sovereign Blockchain Network?
78225.body:
View this post on the web at https://www.team1.blog/p/avalanche-l1-explained-why-build

In the blockchain world, some concepts are used so often that, over time, everyone starts acting as if they already know them. L1 is one of them. Yet when talking about Avalanche today, leaving this concept at the surface means missing the real difference. Because Avalanche approaches the idea of Layer 1 not only as a “main chain,” but as a more flexible and more modular network model.
That is why it is necessary to start with the most basic question first: what is L1?
Want to keep up with the latest in the Avalanche ecosystem? Subscribe to the Team1 blog and get our updates in your inbox weekly.
What Is L1?
In Ethereum’s official What is layer 2? [ https://substack.com/redirect/be628a96-e823-4cde-b0a2-41934370c970?j=eyJ1IjoiMXN4Zm00In0.wehL2Vke0PUDz1PHD6ZKtcy1ufIoeqpblecCEEWPpqI ] explanation, Layer 1 blockchains are defined as the base networks that Layer 2 projects are built on top of, such as Ethereum and Bitcoin. On the same page, it is also explained that Ethereum, as an L1, includes the nodes that validate the network, block producers, transaction history, and the consensus mechanism. To put this in simpler terms, L1 is the main blockchain layer that provides its own security and transaction validation by itself. It does not live on top of another chain, it works by its own rules, and it serves as the foundation for upper-layer solutions.
Today, when most people say L1, they think of a single main network such as Ethereum, Bitcoin, or Avalanche. In other words, the everyday use of the concept mostly rests on the idea of a “base chain.” This is not wrong. However, from this point on, Avalanche takes the concept in a different direction.
What Is Avalanche L1?
According to Avalanche’s official Avalanche L1s documentation [ https://substack.com/redirect/623b49c0-a5f7-4ff1-88fa-2766e617a330?j=eyJ1IjoiMXN4Zm00In0.wehL2Vke0PUDz1PHD6ZKtcy1ufIoeqpblecCEEWPpqI ], an Avalanche L1 is a sovereign network that defines its own membership rules and token economy. This network is validated by a dynamic subset of Avalanche validators and reaches consensus on the state of one or more blockchains. The critical difference here is this: in Avalanche, L1 does not mean only a “single chain.” As clearly stated in the same documentation, while each blockchain is validated by exactly one Avalanche L1, one Avalanche L1 can validate multiple blockchains. As a matter of fact, Avalanche’s own Primary Network [ https://substack.com/redirect/623b49c0-a5f7-4ff1-88fa-2766e617a330?j=eyJ1IjoiMXN4Zm00In0.wehL2Vke0PUDz1PHD6ZKtcy1ufIoeqpblecCEEWPpqI ] is also defined as a special Avalanche L1 and runs three separate chains: P-Chain, C-Chain, and X-Chain.
For this reason, the best way to understand Avalanche L1 is to see it not only as “a main chain,” but as an independent network structure with its own rules, connected to the broader Avalanche ecosystem.

78224.subject: Weekly Recap: The Round Trip
78224.body:
**gm, Defiers!**

Bitcoin finished the week about where it started, after a round trip through $80,000.

The tape ran up into Thursday, when bitcoin cleared $80,000 and **Schwab** said it would add Solana, Avalanche and Chainlink to a retail menu that has carried only bitcoin and ether since May. Friday undid it. **Kevin Warsh** used his first Jackson Hole speech as Fed chair to put the central bank’s focus on prices, saying it has “work to do” on inflation, and bitcoin fell to $76,845.71 before settling near $77,955. Gold dropped 2.35% with it.

**Solana** had the better week. Validators approved doubling the network’s disinflation rate in the first measure to pass through onchain governance, with **Kraken**’s larger validator swinging about 8.1 million SOL from against to for in the closing hours. **Bitwise**’s BSOL became the first Solana ETF past $1 billion. SOL ended the week up about 15%.

The infrastructure news was worse. A shared bug in the **Cosmos EVM** module drained three chains and left two frozen, **Core Lightning** told node operators to go offline with no patch published, and **Moonwell**, **Term Finance** and **The Sandbox** each lost seven or eight figures. Friday closed with an attacker still draining the Solana neobank **Avici**.

In court, the **Ninth Circuit** held that **Kalshi**’s sports event contracts are not swaps, reading the same statute the Third Circuit read in April and reaching the opposite answer.

Enjoy!

———————————————————————————

———————————————————————————

# Top Stories This Week

## Bitcoin Round-Trips $80,000 as Warsh Talks Inflation

Bitcoin cleared $80,000 on Thursday and gave almost all of it back on Friday, [falling as low as $76,845.71 after Kevin Warsh’s first Jackson Hole address as Fed chair](https://thedefiant.io/news/markets/bitcoin-drops-below-usd78-000-after-warsh-speech). “Here is my standard: We must be confident that underlying inflation is moving to our objective, clearly and at sufficient speed,” Warsh said. “Otherwise, we have work to do.” The 12-month change in the PCE price index stands at 3.7% and the six-month change at 4.1%. Bitcoin ended the week at about $77,955, up 0.7% over seven days after touching $81,479.50 overnight Thursday. Gold fell 2.35% and the Nasdaq Composite 0.36% alongside it, and Polymarket now prices a quarter-point September hike at 28% against 1.7% for a cut.

## Solana Validators Cut Emissions in the First Onchain Governance Vote

SGP-0002 [passed with 72.7% support once abstentions were stripped out](https://thedefiant.io/news/blockchains/solana-validators-approve-doubling-disinflation-in-first-governance-vote-with-kraken-reversing), the first measure to clear Solana’s new onchain governance system and the first time validators have agreed to reduce issuance. Six hours before the close it was failing at 65.4%.  There’s a strange little art to spotting AI writing. Large language models enjoy, for instance, using odd phrases like “strange little art”. Yet some of AI’s writing tricks are trickier to catch. Many people believe LLMs stuff their prose with unnecessarily long, grandiloquent words—and use too many em-dashes.
